label: def:LocalRDS
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:LocalRDS}
    Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P,(\theta_t))$ be a MDS. A \emph{continuous local random dynamical system} on $\mathbb R^d$ over this MDS is a map $\varphi:[0,\infty) \times \Omega \times \mathbb R^d_\Delta \to \mathbb R^d_\Delta$ such that the following hold.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] The map $\varphi$ is jointly measurable with respect to $\mathcal B([0,\infty)) \otimes \mathcal F \otimes \mathcal B(\mathbb R^d_\Delta)$.
        \item[(ii)] The state $\Delta \in \mathbb R^d_\Delta$ is a cemetery state, that is, for all $t \geq 0$ and all $\omega \in \Omega$ we have $\varphi(t, \omega, \Delta) = \Delta$.
        \item[(iii)] The map $\varphi$ satisfies the (perfect) cocycle property, that is, for all $t,s \geq 0$, $\omega \in \Omega$ and $x \in \mathbb R^d_\Delta$, we have
        $$\varphi(0, \omega, x) = x \quad \text{and}\quad \varphi(s+t, \omega, x) = \varphi(t, \theta_s \omega, \varphi(s,\omega, x)).$$
        \item[(iv)] For every $\omega \in \Omega$ and every $x \in \mathbb R^d$ the path $t\mapsto \varphi(t, \omega, x) \in \mathbb R^d_\Delta$ is continuous, for every $\omega \in \Omega$ the survival domain 
        $$D_\varphi(\omega) = \{(t,x): \varphi(t, \omega, x) \neq \Delta\}$$
        is open, and for each $\omega \in \Omega$, the map $\varphi(\cdot,\omega, \cdot)|_{D_\varphi(\omega)}$ restricted to the survival domain is jointly continuous. 
    \end{enumerate}
    In the following, we often omit the qualifier ``continuous'' and simply write ``local RDS''.

label: ref:Completion
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{ref:Completion}
    While $\theta$ is jointly measurable with respect to the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal B(\Omega)$, it is not jointly measurable if $\mathcal F$ is replaced by its $\mathbb P$-completion $\bar {\mathcal F}$. This can be seen as follows. Let $B\subset \mathbb R$ be some set that is not Lebesgue measurable and set $f(t) \coloneqq \arctan(t) \,e_1$, where $e_1 \in \mathbb R^d$ is the first unit vector. Clearly $f \in C_0(\mathbb R, \mathbb R^d)$. Set $A \coloneqq \{\theta_t f: t\in B\}$. Since $A$ contains only bounded functions, $A \in \bar {\mathcal F}$. However, $\{(t,g) \in \mathbb R\times C_0(\mathbb R, \mathbb R^d): \theta_t g \in A\}$ is not in $\mathcal B(\mathbb R) \otimes \bar{\mathcal F}$, since its section at $g = f$ is equal to $B$. This issue persists if $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ is replaced by the $\sigma$-algebra of Lebesgue measurable sets.

body_md:
\label{theo:ExistencePullback}
  Suppose that, for the RDS $\varphi$, there exists an absorbing set $B$. Then there exists an (essentially unique) pull-back set attractor $(A(\omega))_{\omega \in \Omega}$, given by
	\[
	A(\omega)
	:=
	\bigcap_{\tau\geq 0}\overline{\bigcup_{t\geq \tau} \varphi\big(t,\theta_{-t}\omega,B(\theta_{-t}\omega)\big)}.
	\]

body_md:
\label{theo:existenceWeakSetAtt}
    Suppose that for every $\varepsilon$, there exists a compact set $C\subset \mathbb R^d$, such that for every bounded set $B\subset \mathbb R^d$, there exists a time $T>0$, such that for all $t>T$ we have
    $$\mathbb P(\varphi(t,\omega, B)\subseteq C)\geq 1-\varepsilon.$$
    Then there exists an (essentially unique) weak set attractor.

title: Proof
body_md:
(i)	From \eqref{Transformation_Evolution} and the definition of $H$, we have
\[
\varphi(t,\omega,x)
=
\Psi(t,\omega,x- O^*(\omega))+ O^*(\theta_t\omega)\,,
\]
which together with the fact that $\Psi$ is a solution of \eqref{RandomDifferentialEquation} implies that
\begin{align*}
\varphi(t,\omega,x)
&=
x- O^*(\omega)
+
\int_0^t G(\theta_s\omega,\Psi(s,\omega,x- O^*(\omega)))\,\mathrm{d} s +  O^*(\theta_t\omega)\\
&=
x+\int_0^t G(\theta_s\omega, H(\theta_s\omega)^{-1}(\varphi(s,\omega,x)))\,\mathrm{d} s+  (O^*(\theta_t\omega)-O^*(\omega))\,.
\end{align*}
Thus, using \eqref{OU_Eq1}, we obtain that
\begin{align*}
\varphi(t,\omega,x)
&=
x
+
\int_0^t G(\theta_s\omega, H(\theta_s\omega)^{-1}(\varphi(s,\omega,x)))-  \alpha O^*(\theta_s\omega)\,\mathrm{d} s +  \omega(t)\\
&=
x+ \int_0^t F(\varphi(s,\omega,x))\,\mathrm{d} s +  \omega(t) \,,
\end{align*}
which completes the proof of this part.

\noindent
(ii) This follows from the definition of a pull-back set attractor and the fact that the shifted term in the transformation $H(\omega, x)$, namely $|O^*(\theta_t\omega)|$, is tempered.

title: Proof
body_md:
Writing $X$ as $(X_1,X_2)^\top$ and $O^*$ as $(O_1^*,O_2^*)^\top$, we rewrite \eqref{RandomDifferentialEquation} as
  \begin{align*}
 \left(
  \begin{array}{l}
  \dot X_1(t)\\
  \dot X_2(t)
  \end{array}
  \right)
  &=
 -
  \left(
  \begin{array}{l}
  X_1(t)+ O_1^*(\theta_t\omega) \\
  X_2(t)+  O_2^*(\theta_t\omega)
  \end{array}
  \right)
  + \alpha
  \left(
  \begin{array}{l}
   O_1^*(\theta_t\omega) \\
   O_2^*(\theta_t\omega)
  \end{array}
  \right)
  \\
  &\quad
  +
  \rho \left( \left|
  \left(
  \begin{array}{l}
  X_1(t)+ O_1^*(\theta_t\omega) \\
  X_2(t)+  O_2^*(\theta_t\omega)
  \end{array}
  \right)
  \right| \right)
  \left(
  \begin{array}{l}
   \phantom{-}X_2(t)+  O_2^*(\theta_t\omega)\\
 -X_1(t)-  O_1^*(\theta_t\omega)
  \end{array}
  \right)\,.
  \end{align*}
    Let $R(t)=\sqrt{X_1(t)^2+X_2(t)^2}$. 
  A direct computation yields
  \begin{align*}
   \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \left(\frac{1}{2} R(t)^2\right)
  = & X_1(t)\dot X_1(t)+ X_2(t)\dot X_2(t)\\
  = &
  -R(t)^2 + (\alpha-1)\,\big(O_1^*(\theta_t\omega) \,X_1(t) +  O_2^*(\theta_t\omega) X_2(t)\big) \\
  &+ \rho \left(\left|
  \left(
  \begin{array}{l}
  	 X_1(t)+ O_1^*(\theta_t\omega) \\
  X_2(t)+  O_2^*(\theta_t\omega)
  \end{array}
  \right)
  \right| \right) \left(   O_2^*(\theta_t\omega) X_1(t) -  O_1^*(\theta_t\omega) X_2(t)\right)\\
   \leq & - R(t)^2+(\alpha-1)\,\big(O_1^*(\theta_t\omega) \,X_1(t) +  O_2^*(\theta_t\omega) X_2(t)\big) \\
 &+ C  \big( 1+R(t)  +  |O^*(\theta_t \omega) |  \big) R(t)\, |O^*(\theta_t \omega) |  \\
   \leq & - R(t)^2 +  \left|\alpha-1\right|\, R(t)\, |O^*(\theta_t \omega) |\\
   &+  C \, |O^*(\theta_t \omega) | \left( R(t) + R(t)^2 + R(t)\, |O^*(\theta_t \omega) |  \right)  \\
  \leq & -  \frac{1}{2} R(t)^2 + \frac 12 \left|\alpha-1\right|^2  |O^*(\theta_t \omega) |^2 \\
  &+  C \, |O^*(\theta_t \omega) | \left( \frac{1}{2} + 2 R(t)^2 + \frac{1}{2}|O^*(\theta_t \omega) |^2 \right),
  \end{align*}
   using Young's inequality for products several times in the last step.
                                               
                               
                  
            
                                              
       
                                                                                                   
                        
          
                    
                                      
                                  
               
           
                                                                                                  
                                                                                                         
                              
                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                        
                
                                                             
  Setting
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:tempered_processes}
    \begin{aligned}
        \gamma(\omega) &\coloneqq \frac{1}{2}\, C\, |O^*(\omega)| + \frac{1}{2} \left|\alpha-1\right|^2  |O^*(\omega) |^2 + \frac{1}{2}\,C\,  |O^*(\omega) |^3, \\
        \beta(\omega) &\coloneqq  -1 + 4 C\, |O^*(\omega) |,
    \end{aligned}
    \end{equation} 
    we can use a comparison argument to obtain for all $t\ge0$, $x\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$ and $\eta_0 \geq |x|^2 $ 
    that $\frac{1}{2}|\Psi(t,\omega,x)|^2\leq \eta(t,\omega,\eta_0)$, where $t\mapsto \eta(t,\omega,\eta_0)$ is the solution~\eqref{Estimate07} to the RDE~\eqref{Estimate_06} with initial value $\eta_0$. 
    This shows the claim.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemm:Ktempered}
    The random variable $L(\omega)$ given by 
$$ L(\omega) \coloneqq \int_{-\infty}^0 \exp\left(\int_s^0 \beta(\theta_u \omega) \,\mathrm{d} u\right) \gamma(\theta_s \omega)\,\mathrm{d} s $$
is tempered.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix some constant $0<c< -\bar \beta$.
Define two random variables $L_1, L_2: \Omega \to [0,\infty]$ by 
\begin{align*}
    L_1(\omega) &\coloneqq \sup_{s \leq 0} \exp\left(-cs+ \int_{s}^0 \beta (\theta_{u} \omega)\, \mathrm{d} u\right)\\
    L_2(\omega) &\coloneqq \int_{-\infty}^0 e^{cs} \gamma(\theta_s \omega) \, \mathrm{d} s
\end{align*}
A simple calculation shows that
\begin{align*}
    L(\omega) &= \int_{-\infty}^0 \exp\left(\int_s^0 \beta(\theta_u \omega) \,\mathrm{d} u\right)\gamma(\theta_s \omega)\,\mathrm{d} s \\
    &= \int_{-\infty}^0 \exp\left(-cs+\int_s^0 \beta(\theta_u \omega) \,\mathrm{d} u\right)e^{cs}\, \gamma(\theta_s \omega)\,\mathrm{d} s \leq L_1(\omega)\, L_2(\omega),
\end{align*}
for each $\omega \in \Omega.$ We complete the proof by showing that both $L_1$ and $L_2$ are tempered.

Let $0<\varepsilon< -\bar \beta -c$. By ergodicity, there exists a full-measure set $\widehat \Omega \subseteq \Omega$ and a random constant $C_\varepsilon(\omega)$, $\omega \in \widehat \Omega$ such that
$$\left|\int_0^t \beta(\theta_s\omega)\, \mathrm{d} s - \bar \beta t\right| \leq C_\varepsilon(\omega) + \varepsilon|t|, \quad \text{for all } t\in \mathbb R, \, \omega \in \widehat \Omega.$$
For any $t\in \mathbb R$ and $\omega \in \widehat \Omega$ we can now bound
\begin{align*}
    \log L_1(\theta_t \omega) &= \sup_{s \leq 0} \left(-cs+ \int_{s}^0 \beta (\theta_{t+u} \omega)\, \mathrm{d} u\right) = \sup_{s\leq t}\left(c(t-s)+\int_{s}^t \beta (\theta_{u} \omega)\, \mathrm{d} u\right)\\
    &= \sup_{s\leq t}\left(c(t-s)+\int_{0}^t \beta (\theta_{u} \omega)\, \mathrm{d} u - \int_{0}^s \beta (\theta_{u} \omega)\, \mathrm{d} u\right) \\
    &\leq \sup_{s\leq t}\big(c(t-s)+\bar \beta (t-s) +\varepsilon (|t|+|s|) +2 C_\varepsilon(\omega)\big)\\
    &\leq \sup_{s\leq t} \big((c+\bar\beta +\varepsilon)(t-s) +2 \varepsilon|t| +2 C_\varepsilon(\omega)\big) =2\varepsilon |t| +2 C_\varepsilon(\omega).
\end{align*}
In particular, we have
$$\limsup_{t \to \pm \infty} \frac{1}{|t|}\log L_1(\theta_t \omega) \leq 2\varepsilon, \quad \text{almost surely}.$$
Since $\varepsilon>0$ can be chosen arbitrarily close to zero, $L_1$ is tempered.

For $L_2$, note that $\gamma$ is a polynomial of $|O^*|$ and hence tempered. Thus, for any $0<\varepsilon<c$, there exist a full measure set $\widetilde \Omega\subseteq \Omega$ and a random constant $C'_\varepsilon(\omega),$ $\omega \in \widetilde \Omega$, such that
$$\gamma(\theta_t \omega) \leq C'_\varepsilon(\omega) \,e^{\varepsilon|t|}, \quad \text{for all } t \in \mathbb R, \, \omega \in \widetilde \Omega.$$
For any $t\in \mathbb R$ and $\omega \in \widetilde \Omega$ we can bound
\begin{align*}
    L_2(\theta_t \omega) &= \int_{-\infty}^0 e^{cs}\,\gamma(\theta_{t+s} \omega) \, \mathrm{d} s =  \int_{-\infty}^t e^{-c(t-s)}\,\gamma(\theta_{s} \omega) \, \mathrm{d} s\leq C_\varepsilon'(\omega) \int_{-\infty}^t e^{-c(t-s) +\varepsilon |s|}\, \mathrm{d} s\\
    &\leq  C_\varepsilon'(\omega) \,e^{\varepsilon|t|}\,\int_{-\infty}^t e^{-(c-\varepsilon)(t-s)}\, \mathrm{d} s = \frac{C_\varepsilon'(\omega)}{c-\varepsilon} e^{\varepsilon|t|}
\end{align*}
In particular, we have
$$\limsup_{t \to \pm \infty} \frac{1}{|t|}\log L_2(\theta_t \omega) \leq \varepsilon, \quad \text{almost surely}.$$
Again, $\varepsilon>0$ can be chosen arbitrarily close to zero, so $L_2$ is tempered as well, completing the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
There exists a local random dynamical system generated by solutions of \eqref{RandomDifferentialEquation}. Due to Lemma~\ref{TechnicalLemma}, the solution $\Psi(t,\omega,x)$, indeed, exists for all $t\ge0$ under assumption~\eqref{eq:PBAtt}. Hence, we can apply Lemma~\ref{TransformSystems} (ii) and it sufficient to show that the random dynamical system  $\Psi$ has a pull-back set attractor. For this, we construct an arbsorbing set and use Theorem \ref{theo:ExistencePullback}.

Let $D(\omega)$  be a tempered random compact set. By definition, there exists a tempered random variable $Q:\Omega\rightarrow (0,\infty)$ and a full-measure set $\widehat \Omega \subseteq \Omega$ such that $D(\omega)\subset B_0({Q(\omega)})$ for all $\omega \in \widehat \Omega$.
Choose again some constant $0<c<-\bar \beta$. By ergodicity and possibly restricting to a smaller full-measure set $\widehat \Omega \subseteq \Omega$, for every $\omega \in \widehat \Omega$ there is a time $t_0 > 0$ such that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ergodicity}
\int_{-t}^0 \beta (\theta_{s} \omega)\, \mathrm{d} s \leq -c\,t, \quad \text{for all } t > t_0.
\end{equation} 
By Lemma~\ref{TechnicalLemma}, for all $t > t_0$ and $x\in D(\theta_{-t}\omega)$, we have 
  \begin{align*}
       |\Psi(t,\theta_{-t}\omega,x)|^2&\leq 2 \eta(t,\theta_{-t}\omega, Q(\theta_{-t}\omega)^2)\\
   &\leq
  2 e^{- c t} Q(\theta_{-t}\omega)^2 + 2 \int_{-t}^0 \exp\left(\int_s^0 \beta(\theta_u \omega) \,\mathrm{d} u\right) \gamma(\theta_s \omega)\,\mathrm{d} s\\
  &\leq
  2 e^{- c t} Q(\theta_{-t}\omega)^2 + 2 L(\omega),
  \end{align*}
  where we use \eqref{Estimate07} to obtain the second inequality.
Since $Q$ is tempered, it follows that $\lim_{t \to \infty} e^{- c t} Q(\theta_{-t}\omega)^2=0$. Define 
  $$\hat R(\omega):=\sqrt{1+2L(\omega)},$$
  which is also tempered.
  There exists $T\geq t_0 >0$ such that
  \[
  \Psi(t,\theta_{-t}\omega,D(\theta_{-t}\omega))
  \subset
  \bar B_0(\hat R(\omega)) \text{ for all } t\geq T,
  \]
  where $\bar B_0(\hat R(\omega))$ denotes the centered closed ball of radius $\hat R(\omega)$. Consequently, $\bar B_0(\hat R(\omega))$ is an absorbing set for each $\omega \in \widehat \Omega$. The existence of a random pull-back set attractor for $\Psi$ follows via Theorem \ref{theo:ExistencePullback} and, hence, we can apply Lemma~\ref{TransformSystems} (ii) to obtain the claim.

title: Proof
body_md:
First note that, by joint continuity of $\varphi(\cdot, \omega, \cdot)$, the process 
    $$(t, \omega) \mapsto \begin{cases} \max_{x\in C_n} |\varphi(t,\omega, x)|,&\text{if } t<\tau^\star(\omega,C_n)\\
    \infty,&\text{otherwise,}
    \end{cases}$$ 
    is continuous as a $[0,\infty]$-valued process and $(\mathcal F_t)$-adapted since the uncountable supremum can be replaced by a supremum over $C_n \cap \mathbb Q^d$. Here, we used the fact that $\tau^\star(\omega,C_n)$ is a $(\mathcal F_t)$-stopping time, see Proposition \ref{prop:tau} (i). Consequently, the random times $\tau^\uparrow_1, \tau^\uparrow_2, \dots$ and $\tau^\downarrow_1, \tau^\downarrow_2, \dots$ are $(\mathcal F_t)$-stopping times. Furthermore, continuity implies
    \begin{align*}
        \tau^\uparrow_n(\omega)<\infty \quad &\Rightarrow \quad \varphi(\tau^\uparrow_n(\omega), \omega, C_n) \subseteq C_{n+1}, \quad \text{and}\\
        \tau^\downarrow_n(\omega)<\infty\quad &\Rightarrow \quad \varphi(\tau^\downarrow_n(\omega), \omega, C_n) \subseteq C_{n-1},
    \end{align*}
    and that these stopping times are almost surely positive.
    
    (i): Since countable intersections of almost sure events are almost sure, it is sufficient to show that for every $n \geq 1$ we have $\mathbb P(\forall\, z \in C_n, \, \tau^\star(\omega, z) = \infty) = 1.$ Let $n \geq 1$. For each $m\geq n$ define a random time $\tau^\uparrow_{n,m}$, recursively, by 
    \begin{align*}
        \tau^\uparrow_{n, n}(\omega) &= 0, \quad \text{and}\\
        \tau^\uparrow_{n,m+1}(\omega) &= \tau^\uparrow_{n,m}(\omega) + \left(\tau^\uparrow_{m}(\theta_{\tau^\uparrow_{n,m}(\omega)}\omega) \wedge t_m\right), ~ \forall \, m \geq n.
    \end{align*}
    According to Proposition \ref{prop:tau} (iii), these are $(\mathcal F_t^+)$-stopping times.
    By construction, we have
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi(t, \omega, C_n) \subseteq B_m, ~ \forall \, t &< \tau^\uparrow_{n,m}(\omega) &&\Rightarrow& \tau^\star(\omega, z) &\geq \tau^\uparrow_{n,m}(\omega), ~\forall \, z \in C_n.
    \end{align*}
    If we can show 
    \begin{equation}\label{waitingtimeconv}
        \sum_{k = n}^\infty \tau^\uparrow_k(\theta_{\tau^\uparrow_{n,k}(\omega)}\omega) \wedge t_k = \lim_{m \to \infty} \tau^\uparrow_{n,m}(\omega) = \infty, \text{ almost surely,}
    \end{equation}
     strong completeness follows. In the following, we write $\tilde \tau^\uparrow_k := \tau_k^\uparrow \circ \theta_{\tau^\uparrow_{n,k}}$ for ease of notation. Note that $\tau_k^\uparrow$ and $\tilde\tau_k^\uparrow$ are identically distributed. By the strong Markov property \eqref{eq:StrongMarkov}, the family of random variables $(\tilde \tau^\uparrow_k \wedge t_k)_{k \geq n+1}$ is independent. Thus \eqref{waitingtimeconv} is a tail event in the sense of Kolmogorov's 0-1-law and it is sufficient to show that \eqref{waitingtimeconv} holds with positive probability. 
     Without loss of generality, we may assume $t_n \leq 1$, as
     $\sum_{n = 1}^\infty t_n = \infty$ also implies $\sum_{n = 1}^\infty (t_n\wedge 1) = \infty$. Now we can bound
     \begin{align*}
         \sum_{k =n}^\infty \tau^\uparrow_k(\theta_{\tau^\uparrow_{n,k}(\omega)}\omega)\wedge t_k =\sum_{k =n}^\infty \tilde \tau^\uparrow_k(\omega) \wedge t_k &\geq \sum_{k =n}^\infty t_k\, \mathds 1_{\tilde \tau^\uparrow_k(\omega) \geq t_k}.
     \end{align*}
     By Kolmogorov's three series theorem, the series on the right hand side diverges with positive probability, as the summands are bounded from above by 1 and satisfy
     \begin{align*}
         \sum_{k =n}^\infty \mathbb E\left[t_k\, \mathds 1_{\tilde \tau^\uparrow_k(\omega) \geq t_k}\right] = \sum_{k =n}^\infty t_k \,\mathbb P\left(\tilde \tau^\uparrow_k(\omega) \geq t_k\right) = \infty.
     \end{align*}
    (ii): The existence of a weak set attractor is established by verifying the conditions of Theorem \ref{theo:existenceWeakSetAtt} and the proof is inspired by the arguments in \cite[Section 7]{LeimbachMattinglyScheutzow22}. We recursively define $(\mathcal F_t^+)_{t \geq 0}$-stopping times (see Proposition \ref{prop:tau} (iii) again) $(\sigma_{n,m}(\omega))_{n \in \mathbb N,\, m \in \mathbb N_0, \, \omega \in \Omega}$ and random variables $(N_{n,m}(\omega))_{n \in \mathbb N,\, m \in \mathbb N_0, \, \omega \in \Omega}$ by $\sigma_{n,0}(\omega) = 0$ and $N_{n,0}(\omega) = n$, for all $n \in \mathbb N$ and all $\omega \in \Omega$, as well as
    $$\sigma_{n,m+1}(\omega) = \sigma_{n,m}(\omega) + \left(\tau^\downarrow_{N_{n,m}(\omega)}(\theta_{\sigma_{n,m}(\omega)}\omega) \wedge \tau^\uparrow_{N_{n,m}(\omega)}(\theta_{\sigma_{n,m}(\omega)}\omega) \wedge t_{N_{n,m}(\omega)}\right)$$
    and
    $$N_{n,m+1}(\omega) = \begin{cases}N_{n,m}(\omega) - 1,& \text{if } \tau^\downarrow_{N_{n,m}(\omega)}(\theta_{\sigma_{n,m}(\omega)}\omega) < \tau^\uparrow_{N_{n,m}(\omega)}(\theta_{\sigma_{n,m}(\omega)}\omega) \wedge t_{N_{n,m}(\omega)} \\
    N_{n,m}(\omega) + 1,& \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
    Since $\tau^\uparrow_n$ and $\tau^\downarrow_n$ are almost surely positive, $\sigma_{n,m}$ is strictly increasing in $m$. Using induction in $m$, one can readily check that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:BallInBall}
        \varphi(t, \omega, C_n) \subseteq B_{N_{n,m}(\omega) +1}, ~\forall\, t \in [\sigma_{n, m}(\omega), \sigma_{n, m+1}(\omega)).
    \end{equation}
    Furthermore, for each fixed $n \in \mathbb N$, the pair $(N_{n,\cdot}, \sigma_{n, \cdot})$ defines a \emph{Markov renewal process} in the sense of \cite[Chapter 10: Definition 1.1]{Cinlar75} (see~also \cite[Definition 7.2]{LeimbachMattinglyScheutzow22}).    
    Thus, the process $(N_{n,\cdot})$ is a discrete time, time homogeneous Markov process with  transition probabilities given by 
    $$\mathbb P\left(N_{n,m+1} = n'-1 \mid N_{n,m} = n'\right) = p_{n'}$$
    and 
    $$\mathbb P\left(N_{n,m+1} = n'+1 \mid N_{n,m} = n'\right) = 1-p_{n'},$$
    where $p_{n'} := \mathbb P (\tau^\downarrow_{n'} < \tau^\uparrow_{n'} \wedge t_{n'})$. In particular, the transition probabilities do not depend on $n$. 
    By \eqref{ineq:ballcritattrcond} there exists a $p^*> \frac{1}{2}$ and an $n^* \in \mathbb N$, such that $p_{n'} \geq p^*$ for each $n'\geq n^*$. Thus, the set $[1, n^*-1] \cap \mathbb N$ is recurrent and for any $n \in \mathbb N$ and for almost every $\omega \in \Omega$ there are infinitely many $m \in \mathbb N_0$ with $N_{n,m}(\omega) \leq n^*-1$. Furthermore, there exists an $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\mathbb P(\tau^\downarrow_{n'} \wedge \tau^\uparrow_{n'} \wedge t_{n'}\geq \varepsilon) \geq \varepsilon$ for all $1\leq n'<n^*$. By the Borel Cantelli Lemma and the strong Markov property, this implies that 
    $\sigma_{n,m+1}-\sigma_{n,m}\geq \varepsilon$ infinitely often almost surely, and consequently
    $\lim_{m \to \infty}\sigma_{n,m}(\omega) = \infty$, for every $n \in \mathbb N$ and almost every $\omega \in \Omega.$ Thus, for each $n \in \mathbb N$ and each $t \geq 0$, the random variable $M_{n,t}: \Omega \to \mathbb N_0$ uniquely given by 
    $$t \in \left[\sigma_{n, M_{n,t}(\omega)}(\omega), \sigma_{n, M_{n,t}(\omega)+1}(\omega)\right)$$
    is well defined for almost every $\omega \in \Omega$. This allows us to introduce the \emph{semi-Markov process} (see \cite[Definition 10.1.15]{Cinlar75}) $(\hat N_{n,t}(\omega))_{n \in \mathbb N, \, t\geq 0, \omega \in \Omega}$ by $\hat N_{n,t}(\omega) := N_{n,M_{n,t}(\omega)}(\omega).$ Now \eqref{eq:BallInBall} can be rewritten as
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:BallInBall2}
        \varphi(t, \omega, C_n) \subseteq B_{\hat N_{n,t}(\omega)+1}, ~\forall\,t\geq 0.
    \end{equation}

    
    Let $\nu_{n,m}$ denote the law of $N_{n,m}$. Standard Markov chain arguments (cf.~e.g.~\cite{MeynTweedie93,BenaimHurth22}) show that there exists a probability measure $\nu$ on $\mathbb N$, which is stationary for the Markov processes $(N_{n,\cdot})$, such that
    $$\nu = \lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{k=1}^m \nu_{n,k}, ~\forall\, n \geq n^*.$$
    Restricting our attention to $n$ which lie in the support of $\nu$, the Markov process $(N_{n,\cdot})$ is irreducible and recurrent. 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
    If the support of $\nu$ is bounded, the conditions of Theorem \ref{theo:existenceWeakSetAtt} can be verified easily, so we assume that $\nu$ has unbounded support. 
    Since $t_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, this implies
    $$\liminf_{m \to \infty} \big(\sigma_{n,m+1}(\omega)-\sigma_{n,m}(\omega)\big) \leq \liminf_{m \to \infty} t_{N_{n,m}(\omega)} = 0,$$
    for all $n \in \operatorname{supp}(\nu)$ and almost every $\omega \in \Omega$. Therefore, the Markov renewal process must be aperiodic and we can invoke \cite[Chapter 10: Theorem 5.22]{Cinlar75} (see~also \cite[Theorem 7.5]{LeimbachMattinglyScheutzow22}) to find that
    $$\lim_{t \to \infty} \mathbb P(\hat N_{n,t} = n') = \tilde \nu(n'), ~\forall\, n' \in \operatorname{supp}(\nu),$$
    where $\tilde \nu$ is the probability measure on $\mathbb N$ given by
    $$\tilde\nu(n) = \left(\sum_{k = 1}^\infty \nu(k)\,\mathbb E[\sigma_{k,1}]\right)^{-1} \nu(n)\, \mathbb E[\sigma_{n,1}].$$
    Note that the sum is finite since $\mathbb E[\sigma_{k,1}]$ can be bounded by $t_k\leq\max_{n \geq 1} t_n < \infty$ and positive since $\nu$ is a probability measure and $\sigma_{k,1}$ is almost surely positive.

 We are now in a position to verify the condition of Theorem \ref{theo:existenceWeakSetAtt}. Let $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $\hat n$ such that $\tilde \nu([1, \hat n]) > 1 - \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and set $C := C_{\hat n+1}$. Let $B \subset \mathbb R^d$ be some bounded set and choose $n \geq n^*$ such that $B \subseteq C_n$. Choose $T \geq 0$ large enough, such that 
  $$\mathbb P(\hat N_{n,t} \leq \hat n) > 1-\varepsilon,~\forall\, t\geq T.$$
 If $\hat N_{n,t} \leq \hat n$, then, by \eqref{eq:BallInBall2}
 $$\varphi(t, \omega, B) \subseteq \varphi(t, \omega, C_n) \subseteq C_{\hat N_{n,t}(\omega)+1} \subseteq C_{\hat n+1} = C,$$
completing the proof.

body_md:
Fix  $b \in \mathbb R$ and $\beta, T\geq 0$. Note that the space $L(b,\beta)$ in \eqref{eq:QDef2} may be replaced by
    $$L_T(b,\beta) := \{\chi: [0,T] \to \mathbb R : (t \mapsto \chi(t)-bt) \in \operatorname{Lip}(\beta)\}.$$
    For every $0\leq s \leq t\leq T$, and every $\chi \in L_T(b,\beta)$, we have 
    \begin{align*}
        &\quad\,\left|\mathcal R(\chi(t))W(t)-\mathcal R(\chi(s))W(s) -\int_{s}^{t} \mathrm{d} \mathcal R(\chi(u))\, W(u)\right|\\
        &=\left|\mathcal R(\chi(t))(W(t)-W(s))+(\mathcal R(\chi(t))-\mathcal R(\chi(s)))W(s) -\int_{s}^{t} \mathrm{d} \mathcal R(\chi(u))\,W(u) \right|\\
        &=\left|\mathcal R(\chi(t))(W(t)-W(s))-\int_{s}^{t} \mathrm{d} \mathcal R(\chi(u))\, (W(u)-W(s))\right|.
                                                                       
                                                                    
    \end{align*}
    In particular, the term is continuous in $\chi$ once $L_T(b,\beta)$ is equipped with the $W^{1,1}$-topology. Since $L_T(b,\beta)$ is separable with respect to that topology, the uncountable supremum in \eqref{eq:QDef2} may be replaced by the supremum over a countable dense subset, giving measurability of $Q_{b, \beta, T}$.

    To show (i) and (ii), note that each function $\chi \in L(b, \beta)$ is $(|b|+\beta)$-Lipschitz continuous. This allows us to estimate
    \begin{align*}
        &\quad\,\left|\mathcal R(\chi(t))(W(t)-W(s))-\int_{s}^{t} \mathrm{d} \mathcal R(\chi(u))\, (W(u)-W(s))\right|\\
        &\leq (1+(t-s)(|b|+\beta)) \sup_{s\leq u \leq t} |W(u)-W(s)|\\
        &\leq 2\,(1+T(|b|+\beta)) \left\|W|_{[0,T]}\right\|_\infty.
    \end{align*}
    In particular, we get
    $$Q_{b, \beta, T} \leq 2\,(1+T(|b|+\beta)) \left\|W|_{[0,T]}\right\|_\infty.$$
    Now, (ii) follows from the fact that Brownian paths are bounded almost surely on compact intervals and (i) from the support theorem for Brownian motion.

body_md:
First, note that by the mean value theorem we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rhoRange}
    {\rho(r) \in [b_n-\beta_n, b_n+\beta_n]}, \quad \forall\, r \in [r_n-3q_n, r_n +q_n]\cap [0,\infty).
\end{equation}

(i): Let $n\geq 1$, $T\geq 0$ and $\omega\in \Omega$ be such that $Q_{b_n, \beta_n, T}< q_n$. Fix an arbitrary $x\in C_n$ and let $X(t) = \varphi(t,\omega,x)$.
Set
$$t^* := T \wedge \inf \{t \in [0,T] : |X(t)|\geq r_n+q_n\}.$$
Our goal is to show that $|X(t^*)| < r_n+q_n$ which implies $t^* = T$ and thus $X(t) \in B_{n+1}$ for all $t \in [0,T]$. 

If $X(t^*) \in C_n$, clearly we are done, so suppose $X(t^*) \notin C_n$. Let $t_0\in [0, t^*)$ be the last time the trajectory leaves $C_n$, that is,
$$t_0 \coloneqq \sup \{t \in [0,t^*] : X(t) \in C_n\}.$$
Set $x_0 \coloneqq X(t_0).$ By the continuity of the trajectory $X$, we have $|x_0|=r_n$. Lemma \ref{lemm:contraction} gives
\begin{align*}
    |X(t^*)| &= |\varphi(t^*-t_0, \theta_{t_0}\omega, x_0)| \leq e^{-(t^*-t_0)}\,|x_0| +\sup_{s \in [0,t^*-t_0]} \left|\int_{s}^{t^*-t_0} \mathcal R(\chi_X(t_0+u)) \,\mathrm{d} W(t_0+u)\right|\\
    &\leq r_n + \sup_{s\in [t_0, t^*]} \left|\int_{s}^{t^*} \mathcal R(\chi_X(u)) \,\mathrm{d} W(u)\right|.
\end{align*}
Since $|X(t)| \in [r_n, r_n+q_n]$ for all $t \in [t_0, t^*]$, we have $\chi_X'(t) \in [b_n-\beta_n, b_n+\beta_n]$ for all $t\in [t_0, t^*]$. In particular, we can find a function $\tilde \chi \in L(b_n,\beta_n)$ that agrees with $\chi_X$ on  $[t_0, t^*]$. We get
\begin{align*}
    |X(t^*)| &\leq r_n + \sup_{s\in [t_0, t^*]} \left|\int_{s}^{t^*} \mathcal R(\tilde \chi(u)) \,\mathrm{d} W(u)\right|\leq r_n +Q_{b_n,\beta_n, T} < r_n +q_n.
\end{align*}


(ii): Let $n\geq 2$ and $\omega\in \Omega$ be such that $Q_{b_n, \beta_n, T_n}< q_n$. Again, fix an arbitrary $x \in C_n$. Our goal is to show $\varphi(T_n, \omega, x) \in C_{n-1}$. Showing this for all $x \in C_n$ gives $\varphi(T_n, \omega, C_n) \subseteq C_{n-1}$. Since (i) additionally gives $\varphi(t, \omega, C_n) \subseteq C_{n+1}$ for all $t \in [0, T_n]$ and in particular $\tau^\star(\omega, C_n) > T_n$, this allows us to conclude the desired bound on $\tau^\downarrow_n(\omega)$.

Again, let $X(t) = \varphi(t,\omega,x)$. By the proof of (i), we have $|X(t)| < r_n+q_n$ for all $t\in [0,T_n]$. We distinguish two cases. First, suppose that $X(t)$ leaves the region where $\rho$ is controlled, that is, $|\varphi(t, \omega, x)| < r_n- 3 q_n$, for some $t \in [0,T_n]$. Let $t_0 \in [0,T_n]$ be the largest such $t$, that is,
$$t_0 := \sup \{t \in [0,T_n] :|X(t)| < r_n- 3 q_n\}.$$
If $t_0 = T_n$, we are done since $r_n-3q_n < r_{n-1}$, so suppose $t_0 < T_n$. Set $x_0 \coloneqq X(t_0)$ and note that, by continuity, $|x_0|= r_n-3q_n$. Also, $$|X(t)| \in [r_n-3q_n, r_n +q_n], \quad \forall \, t \in [t_0, T_n].$$ 
Arguing analogously to (i), we can show
$$|X(T_n)| \leq |X(t_0)| + Q_{b_n, \beta_n, T_n} < r_n -3q_n+q_n \leq r_{n-1}.$$

It remains to treat the case where $X(t)$ does not leave the controlled region, that is, $|\varphi(t, \omega, x)| \in [r_n-3q_n, r_n +q_n]$ for all $t \in [0, T_n]$. Thus $\chi_X'(t) \in [b_n-\beta_n, b_n+\beta_n]$ for all $t \in [0, T_n]$ and there exists a $\tilde \chi \in L(b_n, \beta_n)$ that agrees with $\chi_X$ on $[0, T_n]$. Applying Lemma \ref{lemm:contraction} and using $e^{-T_n} \leq (1+T_n)^{-1}$, we get
\begin{align*}
    |X(T_n)| &\leq e^{-T_n}|X(0)| + \sup_{s \in [0,T_n]} \left|\int_{s}^{T_n} \mathcal R(\tilde \chi(u)) \,\mathrm{d} W(u)\right|\\
    &\leq \frac{1}{1+T_n} r_n + Q_{b_n, \beta_n, T_n} < r_n-3q_n + q_n \leq r_{n-1}.
\end{align*}

i): For $\chi \in L(b,\beta)$ let $\tilde \chi \in L(0,\beta)$ be defined by $\tilde\chi(t) = \chi(t)-bt$. Clearly, the assignment $\chi \mapsto \tilde \chi$ is a bijection between $L(b, \beta)$ and $L(0,\beta)$. Also, define a stochastic process $\widetilde W: [0, T] \to \mathbb R^2$ by 
$$\widetilde W(t) = \int_0^t\mathcal R(bs) \,\mathrm{d} W(s).$$
By rotation invariance $\widetilde W$ is also a Brownian motion, so in particular $W \stackrel{\mathclap{\normalfont\mbox{d}}}{=} \widetilde W$.
In the following, it is convenient to use the expression \eqref{eq:QDef} for $ Q_{b,\beta,T}$. For this, the integral needs to be interpreted as a pathwise integral defined via the integration-by-parts representation \eqref{eq:QDef2}.
Now we have
\begin{align*}
    Q_{b,\beta,T} &= \sup_{0\leq s<t\leq T,\,\chi \in L(b,\beta)} \left|\int_{s}^{t} \mathcal R(\chi(u))\,\mathrm{d} W(u)\right|\\
    &= \sup_{0\leq s<t\leq T,\,\chi \in L(b,\beta)} \left|\int_{s}^{t} \mathcal R(\tilde\chi(u))\mathcal R(bu) \,\mathrm{d} W(u)\right|\\
    &= \sup_{0\leq s<t\leq T,\,\tilde \chi \in L(0,\beta)} \left|\int_{s}^{t} \mathcal R(\tilde \chi(u))\,\mathrm{d} \widetilde W(u)\right|\\
    &\stackrel{\mathclap{\normalfont\mbox{d}}}{=} \sup_{0\leq s<t\leq T,\,\tilde \chi \in L(0,\beta)} \left|\int_{s}^{t} \mathcal R(\tilde \chi(u))\,\mathrm{d} W(u)\right|=Q_{0, \beta, T}.
\end{align*}
ii): Fix $\kappa >0$. For each $\chi \in  L(0,\beta)$ define $\hat \chi \in L(0,\kappa \beta)$ by $\hat \chi(t) = \chi(\kappa t)$. Also define a process $\widehat W$ by $\widehat W(t) = \kappa^{-1/2} \,W(\kappa t)$. Due to the parabolic scaling $\widehat W$ is also a Brownian motion and thus $W \stackrel{\mathclap{\normalfont\mbox{d}}}{=} \widehat W$. Now we have
\begin{align*}
    \kappa^{-1/2} \,Q_{0,\beta, T} &= \sup_{0\leq s<t\leq T,\,\chi \in L(0,\beta)} \left|\int_s^t \mathcal R(\chi(u))\kappa^{-1/2}\, \mathrm{d} W(u)\right|\\
    &= \sup_{0\leq s<t\leq T,\chi \in L(0,\beta)} \left|\int_{\kappa^{-1}s}^{\kappa^{-1}t} \mathcal R(\chi(\kappa u))\kappa^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d} W(\kappa u)\right|\\
    &= \sup_{0\leq \kappa^{-1}s<\kappa^{-1}t\leq\kappa^{-1}T,\,\hat\chi \in L(0,\kappa\beta)} \left|\int_{\kappa^{-1}s}^{\kappa^{-1}t} \mathcal R(\hat\chi(u))\, \mathrm{d} \widehat W(u)\right| \stackrel{\mathclap{\normalfont\mbox{d}}}{=} Q_{0,\kappa \beta, \kappa^{-1}T}.
\end{align*}

Let $\hat \rho(r) := 1\vee \sup_{r'\in [0,r]}|\rho'(r')|$. Suppose \eqref{eq:Compl} holds, that is,
$$\int_0^\infty \hat \rho(r)^{-1/3}\, \mathrm{d} r = \infty.$$
We aim to show strong completeness by invoking Lemma \ref{lemm:ballcrit} (i).
Set $r_1 := 1$ and recursively define $r_{n+1}$ in such a way that $r_{n+1}-r_n = \hat \rho(r_{n+1})^{-1/3}$ holds. This is always possible and the choice is unique since $\hat \rho(r)^{-1/3}$ is monotonically decreasing and continuous. Also $r_n \to \infty$ since otherwise $r_{\infty} \coloneqq \lim_{n \to \infty} r_n<\infty$ would satisfy $\hat \rho(r_{\infty})^{-1/3} = r_{\infty}-r_{\infty} = 0$, leading to a contradiction.

Set
\begin{align*}
    q_n &:= \hat \rho(r_{n+1})^{-1/3},&\beta_n^* &:= 2\hat \rho(r_{n+1})^{2/3}&&\text{and}&t_n &:=\hat \rho(r_{n+1})^{-2/3}.
\end{align*}
 Also let $(b_n)$ and $(\beta_n)$ be the sequences defined in Lemma \ref{lemm:contr2}. By the definition of $\hat \rho$, we have $$\beta_n \leq 2q_n \,\hat \rho(r_n + q_n) = 2q_n \,\hat \rho(r_{n+1}) = 2\hat \rho(r_{n+1})^{2/3} = \beta^*_n.$$
Using Lemma \ref{lemm:contr2} (i) and the monotonicity of $Q_{b,\beta, t}$ with respect to $\beta$, for each $n\geq 1$, we get
$$\mathbb P(\tau_n^{\uparrow}\geq t_n)\geq \mathbb P (Q_{b_n,\beta_n, t_n}<q_n)\geq \mathbb P (Q_{b_n,\beta_n^*, t_n}<q_n).$$
Using Lemma \ref{lemm:QScaling} and Lemma \ref{lemm:youngloeve}, we furthermore get
$$\mathbb P(\tau_n^{\uparrow}\geq t_n)\geq \mathbb P (Q_{b_n,\beta_n^*, t_n}<q_n) = \mathbb P (Q_{b_1,\beta_1^*, t_1}<q_1)>0$$
and thus in particular $\liminf_{n \to \infty}\mathbb P(\tau_n^{\uparrow}\geq t_n)>0$. It remains to show $\sum_{n=1}^\infty t_n = \infty$.
Using the fact that $r_{n+1}-r_n = \hat \rho(r_{n+1})^{-1/3} \leq 1$ and the monotonicity of $\hat \rho$, we can compute
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{n=1}^\infty t_n &=  \sum_{n=1}^\infty \hat \rho(r_{n+1})^{-2/3} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty (r_{n+1}-r_n)\,\hat \rho(r_{n+1})^{-1/3} \\
    &\geq \sum_{n=1}^\infty (r_{n+1}-r_n)\,\hat \rho(r_{n}+1)^{-1/3} \geq \int_1^\infty \hat \rho(r+1)^{-1/3}\, \mathrm{d} r = \infty.
\end{align*}

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that assumptions (i) and (ii) of Lemma \ref{lemm:BlowUpCrit} hold. Fix some natural number $n \in \mathbb N$ and some set $\mathcal M \in \mathcal I_{2n}$, that is, some connected set $\mathcal M$ that intersects $B_1$ and contains at least one point outside $B_{2n}$. The following proof is divided into three steps. First, we set up a recursive scheme, that allows us to treat the continuous time problem as a time-discrete process. There is a possibility that we reach a point at which we are unable to continue this recursion and have to stop. We distinguish between stopping ``successfully'' and stopping ``in failure''. In Step 2 we show that if the recursion does not stop in failure, the set $\mathcal M$ is growing rapidly with respect to $n$. Finally, in Step 3, we find an upper bound for the probability that the recursion stops in failure. Using the result of Step 2, this provides a lower bound for $p_n$.
    
    \textbf{Step 1 -- Introducing the Recursion:}  We start by setting up the recursive scheme, which involves multiple quantities. 
    For this, let $N_0=2n$, $\mathcal M_0 = \mathcal M$, $T_0 = 0$ and choose points $x_0\in B_1 \cap \mathcal M$, $y_0 \in \partial B_{2n}\cap \mathcal M$ and $z_0 \in \partial B_{2n-1}\cap \mathcal M$. Note that such points must exist since $\mathcal M$ is connected. Also, let $(K_i)_{i \in \mathbb N}$ be the deterministic sequence given by $K_i\coloneqq n+\lceil \alpha i\rceil$. The values of $N_i$, $T_i$, $\mathcal M_i$, $x_i$, $y_i$ and $z_i$ will be determined recursively in such a way that $2 \leq N_{i+1} \in \{N_i-1,N_i+1\}$, $T_{i+1}=T_i+\Delta T_{i+1}$ for some $\Delta T_{i+1}>0$ and 
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:recursionCond}
\mathcal M_i = \varphi(T_i,\omega,\mathcal M),\quad
x_i = \varphi(T_i,\omega,x_0) \in C_{K_i}, \quad
y_i \in \partial B_{N_i}\cap \mathcal M_i, \quad
z_i \in \partial B_{N_i-1}\cap \mathcal M_i,
\end{equation}
see Figure \ref{fig:blowupCirt}.
    Furthermore, there is a possibility for the recursion to stop at some iteration $i^*$, after which, for all $i>i^*$, we set $N_i \coloneqq N_{i^*}, T_i \coloneqq T_{i^*},$ and leave the remaining quantities undefined. In this case, we will qualify whether the recursion stopped ``successfully" or ``in failure", which will be relevant for Step 2 below.

    Suppose that after $i$ iterations the recursion did not stop and that $\mathcal M_i, x_i, y_i$ and $z_i$ satisfy \eqref{eq:recursionCond}. Then we set
    $$N_{i+1} \coloneqq \begin{cases}N_i+1, & \text{if } \tau_{N_i+1}(\theta_{T_i}\omega, y_i) \wedge \tau_{N_i+1}(\theta_{T_i}\omega, z_i) \leq \tau_{N_i-1}(\theta_{T_i}\omega, y_i) \wedge t_{N_i},\\
    N_i-1, & \text{otherwise,}
    \end{cases}
   $$
   and $T_{i+1} = T_i +\Delta T_{i+1}$ with
   $$\Delta T_{i+1} \coloneqq \tau_{N_i+1}(\theta_{T_i}\omega, y_i) \wedge \tau_{N_i+1}(\theta_{T_i}\omega, z_i) \wedge \tau_{N_i-1}(\theta_{T_i}\omega, y_i) \wedge t_{N_i} > 0.$$
    If $\tau^\star(\omega, \mathcal M) \leq T_{i+1}$, we stop the recursion successfully. If it did not stop successfully and either $|\varphi(T_{i+1}, \omega, x_0)| >r_{K_{i+1}}$ or ${N_{i+1} \leq K_{i+1}}$, we stop the recursion in failure. Otherwise, we set 
    $${\mathcal M_{i+1} \coloneqq \varphi(T_{i+1}, \omega, \mathcal M) = \varphi(\Delta T_{i+1}, \theta_{T_i}\omega, \mathcal M_i)} \quad\text{and}\quad x_{i+1} =  \varphi(T_{i+1},\omega,x_0) \in C_{K_{i+1}}.$$
    We claim that the set $\mathcal M_{i+1}$ contains at least one point outside $B_{N_{i+1}}$.\\
    \textit{Case 1:} If $N_{i+1} = N_i+1$, then $\Delta T_{i+1}$ is equal to either $\tau_{N_i+1}(\theta_{T_i}\omega, y_i)$ or $\tau_{N_i+1}(\theta_{T_i}\omega, z_i)$ and consequently either 
    $$\varphi(\Delta T_{i+1}, \theta_{T_i} \omega, y_i) \in \partial B_{N_i+1} \cap \mathcal M_{i+1}\quad\text{or}\quad\varphi(\Delta T_{i+1}, \theta_{T_i} \omega, z_i) \in \partial B_{N_i+1} \cap \mathcal M_{i+1}.$$
    \textit{Case 2:} If $N_{i+1} = N_i-1$, since $\Delta T_{i+1} \leq \tau_{N_i-1}(\theta_{T_i}\omega, y_i)$, it follows that $$\varphi(\Delta T_{i+1}, \theta_{T_i} \omega, y_i)\in \mathcal M_{i+1}\setminus B_{N_i-1}.$$
     Since $x_{i+1} \in \mathcal M_{i+1}\cap C_{K_{i+1}} \subseteq \mathcal M_{i+1}\cap C_{N_{i+1}-1}$ and using the fact that $\mathcal M_{i+1}$ is connected, the set $\mathcal M_{i+1}$ must intersect both $\partial B_{N_{i+1}}$ and $\partial B_{N_{i+1}-1}$. This allows us to choose $y_{i+1}$ and $z_{i+1}$ in such a way that $y_{i+1}$ and $z_{i+1}$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{T_{i+1}}$ and satisfy $y_{i+1} \in \partial B_{N_{i+1}}\cap \mathcal M_{i+1}$ and $z_{i+1} \in \partial B_{N_{i+1}-1}\cap \mathcal M_{i+1}$.
    The measurable selection can be achieved, for example, by choosing the smallest elements using the lexicographic ordering of $\mathbb R^d$.
    It is easy to check that $\mathcal M_i$, $x_i$, $y_i$ and $z_i$ satisfy \eqref{eq:recursionCond}, allowing us to continue the recursion.

    \textbf{Step 2 -- Showing Rapid Growth:} Suppose that the recursion does not stop in failure, that is, it either stops successfully or it never stop. We will show that then $\mathcal M$ grows rapidly with respect to $n$. Let $t \geq 0$. We distinguish two cases.
    
    \textit{Case 1:} Suppose that $t<T_\infty \coloneqq \lim_{i \to \infty} T_i$. Then there exists a unique integer $i^*\in \mathbb N_0$, such that $t \in [T_{i^*}, T_{i^*+1})$. In particular, the recursion did not stop at or before step $i^*$. Since $\Delta T_{i+1} \leq t_{N_i}$, $N_i> K_i$, for all $i\leq i^*$, and the sequence $t_n$ is decreasing, we have
    \begin{equation}\label{ineq:TiBound}
        t <T_{i^*+1} = \sum_{i = 0}^{i^*} \Delta T_{i+1} \leq \sum_{i = 0}^{i^*} t_{N_i} \leq \sum_{i = 0}^{i^*} t_{K_i+1} < \frac{1}{\alpha} \sum_{k = n+1}^{K_{i^*}+1} t_{k}. 
    \end{equation}
    Here, the last inequality comes from an elementary computation which we provide in Proposition \ref{prop:elemIneq} below. 
    By the definition of $m(n,t)$ this implies that $m(n,t) \leq K_{i^*} <\infty$.
    If $\tau^\star(\omega, \mathcal M) \leq t$, \eqref{eq:rapidGrow} holds. Otherwise, by the construction of our recursion, we have $\operatorname{rad}(\varphi(t, \omega, \mathcal M) )\geq r_{N_{i^*}-1}$ and $N_{i^*} > K_{i^*}$, so in particular $\operatorname{rad}(\varphi(t, \omega, \mathcal M)) \geq r_{K_{i^*}} \geq r_{m(n,t)}$, establishing \eqref{eq:rapidGrow}.

    \textit{Case 2:} Suppose that $t \geq T_\infty$. If the recursion stops successfully at some step $i^*$, then $\tau^\star(\omega, \mathcal M) \leq T_{i^*}\leq t$, establishing \eqref{eq:rapidGrow}. Hence, we assume that the recursion never stops. Then 
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:bu}
        \limsup_{t \nearrow T_\infty} \operatorname{rad}(\varphi(t, \omega, \mathcal M)) \geq \lim_{i \to \infty} r_{K_i} = \infty.
    \end{equation}
    If $\tau^\star(\omega, \mathcal M)> t\geq T_\infty$, then $\varphi(\cdot, \omega, \cdot): [0,T_\infty] \times \mathcal M \to \mathbb R^d$ is a continuous map that is bounded since its domain is compact. This contradicts \eqref{eq:bu}, so $\tau^\star(\omega, \mathcal M) \leq T_{\infty}\leq t$, establishing \eqref{eq:rapidGrow}.
     
  
    
    
    \textbf{Step 3 -- Bounding the Probability:} We complete the proof by finding an upper bound for the probability that the stops in failure. For this, let $E_0$ be the event in which the recursion stops successfully, and $E_1$ and $E_2$ be the events given by
    \begin{align*}
        E_1 &\coloneqq \{\omega \in \Omega\setminus E_0 : \exists\, i \geq 1,~ |\varphi(T_{i},\omega, x_0)| >r_{K_{i}}\},\text{ and}\\
        E_2 &\coloneqq \{\omega \in \Omega\setminus (E_0\cup E_1) : \exists\, i \geq 1,~ N_i \leq K_i\}.
    \end{align*}
    Clearly, the event that the recursion stops in failure is contained in $E_1 \cup E_2$. In the following, we will show that $\mathbb P(E_1)$ and $\mathbb P(E_2)$ converge to $0$ as $n \to \infty$ uniformly in $\mathcal M$.
    
    We start by bounding the probability for $E_1$. Recalling the estimate \eqref{ineq:TiBound} and the definition of $m(n,t)$, we get $m(n,T_{i+1}) \leq K_{i}\leq K_{i+1}$ for all $i\geq 0$.
    Thus, $E_1$ is contained in the larger event $\tilde E_1\supseteq E_1$ given by
    $$\tilde E_1 \coloneqq \left\{\omega \in \Omega: \exists\, t> 0: |\varphi(t,\omega,x_0)| > r_{m(n,t)}\right\}.$$
    By \eqref{eq:anchorBound} the probability of $\tilde E_1$ goes to $0$ as $n\to \infty$, so the same holds for $E_1$.

    To control the probability for $E_2$, note that, by Proposition \ref{prop:tau} (iii),  $(T_i)_{i\geq 1}$ is a sequence of $(\mathcal F_t^+)$-stopping times and by \eqref{eq:growthBound} and the strong Markov property \eqref{eq:StrongMarkov}, we have
    \begin{align*}
        &\quad~\mathbb E \left[\mathds 1_{N_{i+1}= N_i+1}\mid \mathcal F^+_{T_i}\right](\omega)\\
        &= \mathbb P_{\omega'}\big(\tau_{N_i(\omega)+1}(\omega',y_i(\omega)) \wedge \tau_{N_i(\omega)+1}(\omega',z_i(\omega)) \leq \tau_{N_i(\omega)-1}(\omega', y_i(\omega)) \wedge t_{N_i(\omega)}\big)\geq p^*,
    \end{align*}
    for all $i \geq 0$ and all $\omega$ such that the recursion did not stop before step $i$. Here, $\mathbb P_{\omega'}$ denotes the probability with respect to $\omega'$ for $\omega$ fixed. By a comparison argument, the probability of $E_2$ is upper bounded by the probability
    $$\tilde p_n \coloneqq \mathbb P\left(\exists \,i \geq 1: \tilde N_i\leq K_i \mid \tilde N_0 = 2n\right)\geq \mathbb P(E_2),$$
    where $\tilde N$ is a homogeneous discrete time Markov process on $\mathbb Z$ with 
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb P\left(\tilde N_{i+1} = m+1 \mid \tilde N_i = m\right) &= p^*, \quad\quad \text{ and}\\ 
        \mathbb P\left(\tilde N_{i+1} = m-1 \mid \tilde N_i = m\right) &= 1-p^*.
    \end{align*}
    Clearly, $\tilde N$ has a positive drift with rate $2p^*-1>\alpha$ and $\tilde p_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.
    Thus, we have
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb P(\mathcal M \text{ grows rapidly with respect to } n) &\geq 1 - \mathbb P(E_1) -\mathbb P(E_2)\\
        &\geq 1 - \mathbb P(\tilde E_1) - \tilde p_n \to 1\quad \text{as } n \to \infty,
    \end{align*}
    where the quantity $1 - \mathbb P(\tilde E_1) - \tilde p_n$ is independent of $\mathcal M$. The claim follows.

body_md:
Note that $\tau^\uparrow_1$ and $\tau^\uparrow_2$ are decreasing in $\delta$, so the probability in \eqref{onehalf} is increasing in $\delta$. Thus, we may additionally assume $\delta= 0$ without loss of generality.


The idea of the proof is as follows: For $0<\varepsilon_1\ll 1$ small and $g(R) \in [0,\varepsilon_1]$, the process $R_1(t)$ is a standard Brownian motion with a small negative drift, so its first exit of the interval $[-1,1]$ is via 1 with probability only slightly below 1/2. 
Furthermore, if $ T_1 \gg 1$ is large, this probability of this happening before time $T_1$ is still close to 1/2. More precisely, setting $$p_1(\varepsilon_1, T_1) \coloneqq \inf \mathbb P\left(\tau^\uparrow_1 \leq \tau^\downarrow_1 \wedge T_1\right),$$ where the infimum is over all functions $g$ with $g(R) \in [0,\varepsilon_1]$ for all $R \in [-2,1]$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p1Lim}
    \lim_{\varepsilon_1 \to 0} \,\lim_{T_1\to \infty} p_1(\varepsilon_1,T_1)= \frac{1}{2}.
\end{equation}
Additionally, we consider the probability 
$p_2$ given by $$p_2(\varepsilon_2, T_2) \coloneqq \inf \mathbb P\left(\tau^\uparrow_2 \leq \tau^\downarrow_1\wedge T_2 \text{ and } \tau^\downarrow_1 < \tau^\uparrow_1\right),$$ where the infimum is as in \eqref{newapproach} but with $\varepsilon^*$ replaced by $\varepsilon_2$.

The heart of the proof of Lemma \ref{newapproach} is to show that there exists $\varepsilon^*_2>0$ and $T^*_2>0$ such that $p_2(\varepsilon^*_2, T^*_2) >0$.
Then, by \eqref{eq:p1Lim}, there exists an $\varepsilon_1^*$ and a $T_1^*$ such that $p_1(\varepsilon_1^*, T_1^*) > 1/2 - p_2(\varepsilon^*_2, T^*_2)$. Since both $p_1$ and $p_2$ are decreasing in $\varepsilon_1$, resp.~$\varepsilon_2,$ and increasing in $T_1$, resp.~$T_2$, we can choose $\varepsilon^* \coloneqq \varepsilon_1^* \wedge \varepsilon_2^*$ and $T^* \coloneqq 
T_1^* \vee T_2^*$ and get 
$$p_1(\varepsilon^*, T^*) + p_2(\varepsilon^*, T^*) >1/2.$$
Since the events for $p_1$ and $p_2$ are disjoint and both contained in the event for $p^*$ considered in \eqref{onehalf}, we can conclude
$$p^*\geq p_1(\varepsilon^*, T^*) + p_2(\varepsilon^*, T^*) >1/2.$$

Thus it remains to find $\varepsilon_2^*>0$ and $T_2^*>0$ such that $p_2(\varepsilon^*_2, T^*_2) >0$. For this we use the estimate
\begin{align*}
p_2(\varepsilon_2,T_2)&\geq \inf \mathbb{P}\big(\tau^\uparrow_2 \leq T_2,\, |R_1(s)|\leq \tfrac{1}{3}~ \forall\, s \in [0,T_2], \text{ and } \tau^\downarrow_1 < \tau^\uparrow_1  \, \big)\\
&\geq \frac 13\inf \mathbb{P}\big(\tau^\uparrow_2 \leq T_2 \text{ and }  |R_1(s)|\leq \tfrac{1}{3}~ \forall\, s \in [0,T_2]\, \big) \eqqcolon \frac{1}{3}\, \tilde p_2(\varepsilon_2,T_2),
\end{align*}
where the infimum is as before. The second inequality follows from the fact that the events $\{\omega:\tau^\uparrow_2 \leq T_2\}$ and $\{\omega:|R_1(s)|\leq \tfrac{1}{3},~ \forall\, s \in [0,T_2]\}$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{0,T_2}$ and $R_1(t)$ stopped at $\tau^\downarrow_1 \wedge \tau^\uparrow_1$ is a supermartingale which satisfies
$$\mathbb P \big( \tau^\downarrow_1 < \tau^\uparrow_1\,\big|\,\mathcal F_{0,T_2}\big)\geq \frac{1-R_1(T_2)}{2} \geq \frac{1}{3}, \quad \text{for all } \omega \text{ such that }|R_1(s)|\leq \tfrac{1}{3}~ \forall\, s \in [0,T_2].$$

The following lemma shows that there exists an $\varepsilon_2^*>0$ such that, for $T_2^*=13$, we have $\tilde p_2(\varepsilon_2^*, T^*_2) > 0$ and thus $p_2(\varepsilon_2^*, T^*_2) > 0$, completing the proof.

body_md:
To show \eqref{key},  we represent $R_1(t)$ and $R_2(t)$ in the  form:
\begin{align}\label{umf}
\begin{split}
\mathrm{d} R_1(t)&=- g(R_1(t))\,\mathrm{d} t + \mathrm{d} \overline{W}_1(t),\\
\mathrm{d} R_2(t)&= - g(R_2(t))\,\mathrm{d} t +  \cos(\vartheta(t))\, \mathrm{d}  \overline W_1(t)+\sin(\vartheta(t))\,\mathrm{d} \overline{W}_2(t),\\
\mathrm{d} \vartheta(t) &= \big(h(R_1(t))-h(R_2(t))\big)\,\mathrm{d} t\\ 
&\quad + \gamma(R_2(t))\,\big(  -\sin(\vartheta(t))\,\mathrm{d} \overline W_1(t) +   \cos(\vartheta(t))\,\mathrm{d} \overline W_2(t)\big)  - \gamma(R_1(t))\,\mathrm{d} \overline W_2(t),    
\end{split}
\end{align}
where $\overline {W}_1$ and $\overline{W}_2$ are independent standard Brownian motions given by
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{d} \overline{W}_1(t)&=\cos\big( \phi_1(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d} W_1(t)   +\sin \big( \phi_1(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d} W_2(t),\\
\mathrm{d} \overline{W}_2(t)&=-\sin \big( \phi_1(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d} W_1(t)  +\cos\big( \phi_1(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d} W_2(t) 
\end{align*}
and $\vartheta(t):=\phi_2(t)-\phi_1(t)$.\\  

It will be convenient to represent the system \eqref{umf} in Stratonovich form: 
\begin{align}\label{umfo}
\begin{split} 
\mathrm{d} R_1(t)&=-  g(R_1(t))\,\mathrm{d} t + \mathrm{d} \overline W_1(t),\\
\mathrm{d} R_2(t)&= \Big(- g(R_2(t))  -\frac 12 \gamma(R_2(t)) +\frac 12 \gamma(R_1(t))\cos (\vartheta(t))\Big)\,\mathrm{d} t        \\
& \quad +\cos(\vartheta(t))\circ \mathrm{d} \overline W_1(t)+\sin(\vartheta(t))\circ \mathrm{d}  \overline W_2(t),\\
\mathrm{d} \vartheta(t) &= \Big(h(R_1(t))-h(R_2(t)) -\frac{1}{2}\,\gamma(R_1(t))\,\gamma(R_2(t))\,\sin(\vartheta(t))\Big)\,\mathrm{d} t\\
&\quad + \gamma(R_2(t))\,\big(  -\sin(\vartheta(t))\circ\mathrm{d} \overline W_1(t) +   \cos(\vartheta(t))\circ\mathrm{d} \overline W_2(t)\big)  - \gamma(R_1(t))\circ\mathrm{d} \overline W_2(t).   
\end{split}   
\end{align}


Define 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Tdef}
    \mathcal T:=\inf\Big\{t \geq 0:\vartheta(0)+\big(h(0)-h(-1)\big)t = \frac \pi 2 \mod 2\pi\Big\}.
\end{equation}
The value $\mathcal T$ is chosen so that at time $\mathcal T$ the angular difference $\vartheta_\mathcal T$ mod $2\pi$ is close to  
$\pi/2$ with not too small probability  and so the noise in the radial direction is sufficiently independent for the two trajectories at time $\mathcal T$. 
Recalling the assumptions on $h$, note that $\mathcal T$ depends on the initial value $\vartheta(0)\in [0,2\pi)$ and that $\mathcal T \in [0,4\pi)$, so $\mathcal T+\frac{1}{12} < 13$.

In order to  show the required lower bound for $\tilde p_2$ we consider the (deterministic) solution $(\hat R_1, \hat R_2, \hat \vartheta)$ of 
\eqref{umfo} with $\overline W_1$ replaced by 0 and $\overline W_2$ replaced by the path that takes the value 0 on $[0,\mathcal T]$ and the value $36(t-\mathcal T)$ for $t \geq \mathcal T$. Observe that in this way the process 
$\hat R_2(t)$ experiences a strong upward kick after time $\mathcal T$ causing $\hat R_2(t)$ to pass $\hat R_1(t)$. We must ensure that the solution of the (random) equation \eqref{umfo} remains close to $(\hat R_1, \hat R_2, \hat \vartheta)$ on $[0,\mathcal T]$ with probability bounded away from 0 uniformly with respect to the choice of the coefficients. To obtain such bounds we use results from rough paths theory. 

\textbf{Step 1 -- Deterministic Control via Rough Paths Theory:}
Let $\overline {\bf W}=(\overline {W}, \overline{\mathbb{W}})$ be the geometric rough path obtained from the 2-dimensional Brownian motion $\overline W$ enhanced with $\overline{\mathbb{W}}:= \overline{\mathbb{W}}^{\textrm{Strat}}$ (see \cite[Proposition 3.5]{FrizHairer1}). 
For some $\alpha \in \big(\frac 13,\frac 12\big)$,  which we fix for the remainder of the proof, we consider $\overline {\bf W}$ as a random element of the space ${\mathscr{C}}_{\operatorname g,0}^{0,\alpha}\big([0,13],\mathbb{R}^2\big)$ of $\alpha$-H\"older geometric rough paths starting at 0 and equipped with the $\alpha$-H\"older rough path metric $\varrho = \varrho_{\alpha,13}$ (see \cite[Definition 2.3]{FrizHairer1} or \cite[Definition 2.4]{FrizHairer2}). The letter $\operatorname g$ in ${\mathscr{C}}_{\operatorname g,0}^{0,\alpha}$ stands for {\em geometric} and has nothing to do with the function $g$.
For each  $T \in [0,13]$, the support of the law of $\overline {\bf W}$  contains the geometric rough path ${\bf U}_T=\big(U_T,\mathbb{U}_T\big)$ generated by $U_T(t)=(0,36(t-T)_+)^\top\coloneqq(0,0 \vee 36(t-T))^\top$, $t \in [0,13]$, defined as
$$U_T(s,t) = U_T(t)-U_T(s) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbb U_T(s,t) = \frac{1}{2}U_T(s,t) \otimes U_T(s,t),$$
see \cite[Exercise 9.6]{FrizHairer1} or \cite[Theorem 13.54]{FrizVictoir}. Following the discussion above, we are particularly interested in $\mathbf U_{\mathcal T}$ for $\mathcal T$ defined in \eqref{eq:Tdef}. Since the set $\mathcal U \coloneqq \{\mathbf U_T : T \in [0, 13]\}$ is compact in ${\mathscr{C}}_{\operatorname g,0}^{0,\alpha}\big([0,13],\mathbb{R}^2\big)$, for each $D>0$, it can be covered with finitely many balls of radius $D/2$ and center in $\mathcal U$. Such balls have a positive mass under the law of $\overline{\bf W}$ and hence, for every $D>0$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{Kuh}
    Q(D):=\inf_{T \in [0,13]}\mathbb{P} \big(\varrho\big( \overline {\bf W}   , {\bf U}_T   \big)\leq D\big)>0.
\end{equation}
 The {\em It\^o-Lyons map} maps a rough path ${\bf V}=(V,\mathbb{V})$ in ${\mathscr{C}}_{\operatorname g,0}^{0,\alpha}\big([0,13],\mathbb{R}^2\big)$ to the solution $ Y^{\bf V}=(R_1^{\bf V}, R_2^{\bf V},\vartheta^{\bf V} )$ of the rough differential equation (RDE) associated to \eqref{umfo}, with $\overline {\bf W}=(\overline {W}, \overline{\mathbb{W}})$ replaced by ${\bf V}=(V, \mathbb{V})$ and with initial condition $(R_1^{\bf V}(0), R_2^{\bf V}(0),\vartheta^{\bf V}(0)) = (0,-1, \phi_2^0-\phi_1^0)$ as above. This map is continuous with respect to $\varrho$ (see \cite[Theorem 8.5]{FrizHairer1} or \cite[Theorem 8.5]{FrizHairer2}) but we need more detailed information on how the modulus of continuity depends on $g$, $h$, $\gamma$, and $\vartheta(0) = \phi_2^0-\phi_1^0$. 
Such a quantitative continuity result is Theorem \ref{RoughDE} which is a special case of \cite[Theorem 12.10]{FrizVictoir}.                          
 In order to apply Theorem \ref{RoughDE}  we  extend the range of $\vartheta$ from $S^1$ to $\mathbb{R}$ in a periodic manner and only consider the case $\Gamma = \mathbb{R}$, see Remark \ref{Upsilon}. We have
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:itoLyonsStab}
     \sup_{0 \leq t \leq 13} |Y^{\bf V}(t)-Y^{{\bf U}_{\mathcal T}}(t)| \leq C  \varrho ({\bf V},{\bf U}_{\mathcal T}),
 \end{equation}
 where $C$  depends only on $\alpha$, upper bounds for
  $\varrho ({\bf V},{\bf 0})$, $\varrho ({\bf U}_{\mathcal T},{\bf 0})$, and on an upper bound for the supremum norms of $|g|,|g'|,|g''|,|\gamma|,|\gamma'|,|\gamma''|,|\gamma'''|$, $|h|$, $|h'|$, and $|h''|$. By Remark \ref{Upsilon} we can assume, without loss of generality, that the latter are upper bounded by some universal constant $\Upsilon \geq 3$.
    Since $\mathcal U \coloneqq \{\mathbf U_T : T \in [0, 13]\}$ is compact, we have $\sup_{T \in [0, 13]}\varrho(\mathbf U_T, \mathbf 0) <\infty$ and the constant in \eqref{eq:itoLyonsStab} can be chosen to depend only on $\varrho({\bf V},{\bf 0})$. In particular, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{estim}
  \sup_{0 \leq t \leq 13} |Y^{\bf \overline{W}}(t)-Y^{{\bf U}_{\mathcal T}}(t)| \leq C(\varrho({\bf \overline{W}},{\bf 0}))\,\varrho ({\bf \overline{W}},{\bf U}_{\mathcal T}),
  \end{equation}
  where $C$ is increasing in its argument. For $\varrho ({\bf \overline{W}},{\bf U}_\mathcal T) \leq 1$, we have
  $$C(\varrho ({\bf \overline{W}},{\bf 0})) \leq C(\varrho ({\bf U}_\mathcal T,{\bf 0})+1).$$
  In particular, for every $\eta >0$, there exists a $D(\eta)\in (0, 1]$, depending only on $\eta$, such that
  $$\varrho ({\bf \overline{W}},{\bf U}_\mathcal T) \leq D(\eta) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \sup_{0 \leq t \leq 13} |Y^{\bf \overline{W}}(t)-Y^{{\bf U}_\mathcal T}(t)| \leq \eta.$$
  Since $Y^{\bf \overline {W}}$ coincides with the Stratonovich solution $Y = (R_1, R_2, \vartheta)$ of  \eqref{umfo} (see \cite{FrizVictoir}), we have
  \begin{align*}
      \mathbb P\left(\sup_{0 \leq t \leq 13} |Y(t)-Y^{{\bf U}_\mathcal T}(t)| \leq \eta\right) &= \mathbb P\left(\sup_{0 \leq t \leq 13} |Y^{\bf \overline{W}}(t)-Y^{{\bf U}_\mathcal T}(t)| \leq \eta\right)\\
      &\geq \mathbb P \left(\varrho ({\bf \overline{W}},{\bf U}_\mathcal T) \leq D(\eta)\right) \geq Q(D(\eta)),
  \end{align*}
  where the right-hand side is positive and depends only on $\eta$. 
  
      For simplicity, we write $$Y^{{\bf U}_\mathcal T}=(R_1^{{\bf U}_\mathcal T}, R_2^{{\bf U}_\mathcal T},\vartheta^{{\bf U}_\mathcal T}) \eqqcolon (\hat R_1, \hat R_2, \hat \vartheta).$$
Our goal is to show that there exist universal constants $0<\varepsilon<1$ and $0 < \eta < \frac{1}{6}$ such that for $g, h$ and $\gamma$ satisfying (\ref{eq:gCond}--\ref{eq:gammaCond}) with $\varepsilon^*$ replaced by $\varepsilon$, we have
 \begin{align}
      |\hat R_1(t)| \leq \frac{1}{6},~ \forall \, t\in [0,13], \label{eq:R1U}\\
      \exists\, t' \in [0, \tfrac{1}{12}], \text{ s.t. }\hat R_2(\mathcal T+t') = 1+ \eta \quad \text{and}\quad  \hat R_2(t) \geq -\frac{11}{6},\quad\forall\, t\in [0, \mathcal T+t'].\label{eq:R2U}
  \end{align}
Once this is established, we have the implication
$$\sup_{0 \leq t \leq 13} |Y(t)-Y^{{\bf U}_\mathcal T}(t)| \leq \eta\quad \Rightarrow\quad \tau^\uparrow_2 \leq 13,\text{ and } |R_1(t)|\leq \tfrac 13 ~ \forall\, t \in [0,13],$$
and thus
$$\mathbb{P}\Big(\tau^\uparrow_2 \leq 13,\text{ and } |R_1(t)|\leq \tfrac 13 ~ \forall\, t \in [0,13]\Big)\geq Q(D(\eta))>0.$$
Since $Q(D(\eta))$ is independent of $g,h,\gamma,\phi_1^0$ and $\phi_2^0$, the infimum in \eqref{key} is positive as well. 
Thus it remains to prove \eqref{eq:R1U} and \eqref{eq:R2U} for appropriately chosen $\varepsilon$ and $\eta$.
  \paragraph{Step 2 -- Estimates for the Deterministic Trajectory:}

We have
    \begin{align*}
\begin{split} 
\mathrm{d} \hat R_1(t)&=-  g(\hat R_1(t))\,\mathrm{d} t\\
\mathrm{d} \hat R_2(t)&= \Big(- g(\hat R_2(t))  -\frac 12 \gamma(\hat R_2(t)) +\frac 12 \gamma(\hat R_1(t))\cos (\hat \vartheta(t))\Big)\,\mathrm{d} t   +\mathds 1_{t \geq \mathcal T}\,36\sin(\hat \vartheta(t)) \,\mathrm{d} t,\\
\mathrm{d} \hat \vartheta(t) &= \Big(h(\hat R_1(t))-h(\hat R_2(t)) -\frac{1}{2}\,\gamma(\hat R_1(t))\,\gamma(\hat R_2(t))\,\sin(\hat \vartheta(t))\Big)\,\mathrm{d} t\\
&\quad +\mathds 1_{t \geq \mathcal T}\,36 
\big(\gamma(\hat R_2(t))\,\cos(\hat\vartheta(t)) - \gamma(\hat R_1(t))\big)\, \mathrm{d} t, 
\end{split}   
\end{align*}
with $(\hat R_1(0), \hat R_2(0), \hat \vartheta(0)) = (0,-1, \vartheta(0))$.
Clearly,
$|\hat R_1(t)| \in [0,13\, \varepsilon]$, for all $t\in [0,13]$.
Thus \eqref{eq:R1U} holds as long as $13\,\varepsilon \leq 1/6.$ For \eqref{eq:R2U}, we need to treat the time intervals $[0, \mathcal T]$ and $[\mathcal T, \mathcal T+ \tfrac{1}{12}]$ separately. For $t \leq \mathcal T$, we have $$|\hat R_2(t)+1| \in [0,2\mathcal T \varepsilon] \subseteq [0, 26\,\varepsilon].$$
Furthermore, we have
\begin{align*}
    \hat \vartheta(\mathcal T) &= \vartheta(0) + \int_0^\mathcal T\Big(h(\hat R_1(t))-h(\hat R_2(t)) -\frac{1}{2}\,\gamma(\hat R_1(t))\,\gamma(\hat R_2(t))\,\sin(\hat \vartheta(t))\Big)\,\mathrm{d} t\\
    &= \vartheta(0) + (h(0) - h(-1)) \mathcal T + \int_0^\mathcal T \big(h(\hat R_1(t))-h(0)\big)\, \mathrm{d} t - \int_0^\mathcal T \big(h(\hat R_2(t))-h(-1)\big)\, \mathrm{d} t\\
    &\quad - \int_0^{\mathcal T}\frac{1}{2} \,\gamma(\hat R_1(t))\,\gamma(\hat R_2(t))\,\sin(\hat \vartheta(t))\,\mathrm{d} t.
\end{align*}
Recall from \eqref{eq:Tdef}, that $\mathcal T$ was defined in such a way that 
$$\vartheta(0) + (h(0) - h(-1)) \mathcal T = \frac{\pi}{2},\quad \text{mod } 2\pi.$$
Since the lift of the initial value $\vartheta(0)$ from $S^1$ to $\mathbb R$ was arbitrary, we may assume without loss of generality that this equality holds in $\mathbb R$ as well.
Using the previous estimates on $|\hat R_1(t)|$ and $|\hat R_2(t)+1|$ and the fact that the derivative of $h$ is at most $3/2$ on $[-2,1]$, we get
\begin{equation}\label{eq:thetaOfT}
    \left| \hat \vartheta(\mathcal T) - \frac{\pi}{2}\right| \leq 13\, \varepsilon\, \frac{3}{2}\, \mathcal T + 26\, \varepsilon\, \frac{3}{2}\, \mathcal T + \frac{1}{2}\, \varepsilon^2\, \mathcal T\leq 767\,\varepsilon.
\end{equation}


Note that to show \eqref{eq:R2U}, we are required to control the trajectory of $\hat R_2$ after it leaves the interval $[-2,1]$ on which $g, h$ and $\gamma$ are controlled by (\ref{eq:gCond}--\ref{eq:gammaCond}). Here, the fact that $|g'|, |h'|$ and $|\gamma'|$ are globally bounded by the universal constant $\Upsilon\geq 3$ is useful. By choosing $\eta \coloneqq \varepsilon/ \Upsilon$, for $\varepsilon$ still to be determined, the intermediate value theorem gives 
$$|g(r)| \leq 2\varepsilon, \quad|h(r)| \leq 3+\varepsilon<4, \quad\text{and}\quad |\gamma(r)|\leq 2\varepsilon, \quad \forall\, r \in [-2,1+\eta].$$
Let $t^* \in (0,\tfrac{1}{12}]$ be the given by
$$t^*\coloneqq \frac{1}{12} \wedge \inf \{t\geq 0: \hat R_2(\mathcal T+ t) \notin [-2, 1+\eta]\}.$$
We  can control the trajectory of $\hat \vartheta$ on the interval $[\mathcal T, \mathcal T + t^*]$. For $t \in [0, t^*]$, we have
\begin{align*}
    \left|\hat \vartheta(\mathcal T+t) -\hat \vartheta(\mathcal T)\right| &\leq \int_\mathcal T^{\mathcal T+t}\Big|h(\hat R_1(s))-h(\hat R_2(s)) -\frac{1}{2}\,\gamma(\hat R_1(s))\,\gamma(\hat R_2(s))\,\sin(\hat \vartheta(s))\Big|\,\mathrm{d} s\\
    &\quad + 36\int_\mathcal T^{\mathcal T+t} 
\big|\gamma(\hat R_2(s))\,\cos(\hat\vartheta(s)) - \gamma(\hat R_1(s))\big|\, \mathrm{d} s\\
&\leq \frac{1}{12} \,(4+4+2\varepsilon^2) + \frac{36}{12}\cdot 4\varepsilon \leq \frac{2}{3} + 13 \varepsilon.
\end{align*}
Together with \eqref{eq:thetaOfT}, and requiring $\varepsilon$ to be very small ($\varepsilon\leq 10^{-4}$ suffices), we get
$$ \left|\hat \vartheta(\mathcal T+t) -\frac{\pi}{2}\right| \leq \left|\hat \vartheta(\mathcal T) -\frac{\pi}{2}\right| +\left|\hat \vartheta(\mathcal T+t) -\hat \vartheta(\mathcal T)\right| \leq \frac{2}{3} + 780\,\varepsilon \leq \frac{\pi}{4}, \quad \forall \, t \in [0, t^*].$$
In particular, we have $\sin(\hat \vartheta(t)) \geq \sqrt 2/2$ for $t \in [\mathcal T, \mathcal T + t^*]$.
This bound allows us to finally control the trajectory of $\hat R_2$ on the interval $[\mathcal T, \mathcal T + t^*]$. For $t \in [0, t^*]$, we have
\begin{align*}
    \hat R_2(\mathcal T+ t) &\geq \hat R_2(\mathcal T) + \int_\mathcal T^{\mathcal T+t}\Big(- g(\hat R_2(s))  -\frac 12 \gamma(\hat R_2(s)) +\frac 12 \gamma(\hat R_1(s))\cos (\hat \vartheta(s))\Big)\,\mathrm{d} s \\
    &\quad +36\int_\mathcal T^{\mathcal T+t}\sin(\hat \vartheta(s)) \,\mathrm{d} s\\
&\geq -1-26\,\varepsilon - \frac{1}{12}\cdot 4\,\varepsilon +36 \, t \, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \geq -1 - 27 \,\varepsilon + 25\, t.
\end{align*}
For $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small, we can deduce that $\hat R_2(t)\geq -11/6$ during $[\mathcal T, \mathcal T+t^*].$ Furthermore, if $\varepsilon$ is small enough such that $-1-27\varepsilon +25/12 > 1+ \varepsilon/3 \geq 1+\eta$, by the definition of $t^*$, we know that $t^* < 1/12$, and hence $\hat R_2(\mathcal T + t^*) = 1+\eta$. This establishes \eqref{eq:R2U} and thereby the proof of Lemma \ref{Key} and Lemma \ref{newapproach}.

body_md:
\label{RoughDE} Let $\alpha \in \Big(\frac 13,\frac 12\Big)$ and $T>0$. 
Let ${\bf{U}}=(U,{\mathbb{U}})$ and ${\bf{V}}=(V,\mathbb{V})$ belong to the class $\mathscr{C}^{0,\alpha}_{g,0}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^d)$ of geometric rough paths starting at 0 and equipped with the  $\alpha$-H\"older rough path metric $\varrho_{\alpha, T}$. Let ${\bf Y^U}=\big(Y^{\bf U},\mathbb{Y^{\bf U}})$ be the solution of the rough differential equation
\begin{equation}\label{roughSDE}
\mathrm{d} Y(t)=A(Y(t))\,\mathrm{d} t+ B(Y(t))\,\mathrm{d} {\bf U}(t),\quad Y(0)=y_0\in \mathbb{R}^e,
\end{equation}
(and similarly for ${\bf V}$ instead of ${\bf U}$), where $A\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^e,\mathbb{R}^e)$ and $B \in C^3(\mathbb{R}^e, \mathbb{R}^{e\times d})$ are such that $B$ together with its derivatives up to order 3 and $A$ together with its derivatives up to order 2 are bounded by a number $M$. 

Then
$$
\sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} |Y^{\bf V}(t)-Y^{\bf U}(t)|\leq C \varrho_{\alpha,T}(\bf{V},\bf{U}),
$$
where $C$ depends on $\alpha$,  $M$, $d$, $e$, and upper bounds of $T$, $\varrho_{\alpha,T}({\bf U},{\bf 0})$, and  $\varrho_{\alpha,T}({\bf V},{\bf 0})$ only.
